citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility is not providing adequate veterinary care to the animals. Three previously identified chinchillas in the second
building of the facility that required veterinary care are not currently receiving any medical treatment to alleviate pain and
discomfort.
- A white and gray chinchilla (#0018) first identified by APHIS personnel on 5-August-2026 with eye issues was observed
with severe swelling and yellow pus-like discharge exuding from both eyes. Both eyes are swollen shut and the animal
appears unable to open them preventing observation of the globes of the eye. The facility representative stated this
animal was initially treated with neomycin/polymyxin B/dexamethasone topical ointment as directed by the Attending
Veterinarian (AV) starting on 07-August-2026. The eyes showed no improvement while treating with the topical ointment
according to the representative. The representative stated after consulting with the AV based on culture and sensitivity
results the AV recommended switching to ofloxacin ophthalmic solution as treatment. The representative stated the
animal was treated for an additional 5 days and the eyes appeared to worsen while on this medication so it was
discontinued on approximately 23-August-2026. The animal did not receive any further treatment and was not re-
evaluated by the AV until 8/31/2026 at which time humane euthanasia was recommended. This animal is currently
receiving no treatments to alleviate pain and discomfort.
- A gray chinchilla first identified by APHIS personnel on 5-August-2026 (DFH previously identified as L2) was observed
with clear discharge from the mouth causing the fur in the chin and neck area to appear wet. The animal has an unkept
appearance with a poor haircoat. Additionally, there was a visible protrusion on both sides of the back of the lower jaw
that could be observed by APHIS personnel. This was determined to be caused by malocclusion according to the facility
representative. The animal was not re-evaluated by the AV until 31-August-2026 at which time humane euthanasia was
recommended. This animal is currently not receiving any treatment to alleviate pain and discomfort.
-A grey chinchilla (J1143) located in 15-I-middle was observed with thick lumps of matted fur encompassing nearly the
entire hind end of the body. This individual was identified on the previous inspection report on 11-August-2026 and was
evaluated by the AV but had not been treated for this condition.
Correct by ensuring that the animals previously identified and evaluated by the Attending Veterinarian are provided the
appropriate treatment for their medical conditions as prescribed by 9:00 pm on 2-September-2026.
Additionally, the following animals were identified in the second building of the facility requiring veterinary care:
- A standard gray chinchilla M1010 was observed with generalized strands of matted fur on the hind end. The fur near the
left side of the base of the tail appears to contain brown organic material impacted in the matted fur.
-A grey chinchilla (H802) was observed with excessive matting on the animals back extending to the base of the tail.
There was light brown staining in the fur near the base of tail and extending up the right side of the animal.
-A ebony angora chinchilla with a label of (h1225) on the enclosure had string like mats and an unkept hair coat.
- A white chinchilla (F1111) had excessive string like matting primarily on the back creating a mohawk like appearance
starting from the base of neck to the animals hind end.
- A male grey standard chinchilla located in row 13 had a large mat encompassing the mid back to the base of the tail.
The mat appeared to be thick and had yellow staining, brown organic material, and bedding throughout the matted area.
The base of the underside of the tail appeared wet and the fur was stained light brown.
Failure to provide appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries can lead to
worsening of medical conditions resulting in unnecessary pain and distress to the animals.
Additionally, correct by ensuring the animals identified and listed above are physically evaluated by the attending
veterinarian so that the animals can be properly examined, diagnosed, and treated. Correct by, 02-September-2026 at
9:00 PM.

The facility does not have an accurate record of all acquisitions for regulated animals. The records of animals on hand are
still missing the adult chinchillas that are currently being housed in Building #2.
Improper recordkeeping does not allow APHIS officials to properly account for animals on the premises or allow for proper
tracking of animals. Each dealer and exhibitor shall make, keep, and maintain records or forms which fully and correctly
disclose all information required by the AWA concerning each animal purchased or otherwise acquired, owned, held, or
otherwise in his or her possession or under his or her control, or which is transported, euthanized, sold, or otherwise
disposed of by that dealer or exhibitor.

The second building is not being adequately maintained in good repair, is not structurally sound, and does not protect the
animals from injury:
-In the far side of the building, there is a section of the ceiling that is caving in onto a row of enclosures housing some
animals and enclosures that could potentially house animals. The ceiling appears to be caving in about 1 foot with a
noticeable bend in the structure.
-In the majority of enclosures, there were jagged edges found in the metal feeders and dust baths.
-There were various sharp points on metal wiring of the enclosure fronts, doors, and walls of enclosures.
-A few enclosures contained floors that were falling apart due to rust forming sharp points.
Failure to maintain housing facilities in structurally sound condition and in good repair could result in the ceiling falling
onto the enclosures causing injury to the regulated animals. Jagged edges could also result in injury to the regulated
animals. The facility must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved.
Correct by ensuring housing facilities shall be structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the
animals from injury and to contain the animals.

While the facility did install additional fans to aid in ventilation there remains a strong odor of ammonia present in the
second building animal housing area. There are numerous animals in this building that are being treated for ocular issues.
High levels of ammonia can cause discomfort to the animals and lead to further health issues. The facility must ensure
indoor housing facilities shall be adequately ventilated by natural or mechanical means to provide for the health and to
prevent discomfort of the animals at all times. Such facilities shall be provided with fresh air either by means of windows,
doors, vents, fans, or air-conditioning and shall be ventilated so as to minimize drafts, odors, and moisture condensation.

The facility is not adequately cleaning enclosures:
-In the second building, an enclosure in row 13 containing one chinchilla had excessive buildup of fecal material
encompassing almost the entire floor of the enclosure with minimal to no clean bedding.
-In the second building, an enclosure containing two grey chinchillas (L264, K1181) had excessive buildup of fecal
material encompassing almost the entire floor of the enclosures with minimal to no clean bedding.
- In the second building, one enclosure containing one adult chinchilla and two kits and another enclosure containing one
adult chinchilla and one kit had excessive buildup of fecal material encompassing almost the entire floor of the enclosure
with minimal to no clean bedding.
- In the second building, an enclosure in row 15 had an excessive buildup of wet substrate encompassing almost the
entire floor of the enclosure with minimal to no clean or dry bedding.
-In the first building, in room 3, row 2, an enclosure containing one black chinchilla had excessive buildup of fecal material
encompassing the entire floor of the enclosure and nest box with minimal to no clean bedding.
As a result, the animals must walk through the fecal material and wet substrate to gain access to both their food and
water. Accumulations of feces, urine, and soiled bedding are harmful to the animals as they can spread disease, attract
pests, and cause unpleasant odors. Additionally, due to this species’ natural history an excessively wet and moist
environment can be detrimental to the health and well-being of the animals. Excreta shall be removed from primary
enclosures as often as necessary to prevent contamination of the animals contained therein and to minimize disease
hazards and to reduce odors. Correct by 9 pm 2-SEP-2026.

In the second building, the facility is not adequately cleaning the premises:
-There is an excess of discarded bedding and fecal material on the floors between the rows of animal enclosures. There
are excessive amounts of cobwebs observed throughout the facility including on top of and behind the enclosures.
-Multiple enclosures were observed with clumps of hair from the animals trapped in the wire fencing in both the front and
rear of the enclosures. Hair was also seen caught on the automatic watering lines. Unused enclosures and runs that
attach multiple enclosures for breeding contain multiple cobwebs trapping debris. There are less cobwebs observed in the
front section of the second building, however there are still excessive cobwebs throughout the back section of the
building. Spaces in this building not currently being used to house animals are cluttered with accumulation of trash, dust,
debris, soiled animal bedding, cobwebs, equipment, and miscellaneous items.
-Most of the ceiling panels in the second building have areas of severe accumulations of dark brown, black, and white
staining.
Failure to adequately clean the animal enclosures and the premises can lead to illness, transmission of diseases, and
attract unwanted pests. The facility must ensure that the premises are kept clean and in good repair to protect the animals
from injury to facilitate the prescribed husbandry practices set forth in this subpart.

An effective pest control method is not being utilized at the facility. There were too numerous to count spiders located
throughout the facility, with numerous spiders found in close proximity to the animals. Failure to ensure facility is free from
pests could result in injury or disease transmission to the regulated animals. A safe and effective program for the control
of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
Jonathan Tomkovitch, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER
Eric Irvin, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
